paragraphs.heading: What a volcano is
paragraphs.text: A volcano is a vent or crack in the crust of a planet-sized body. Through it, hot lava, volcanic ash and gases escape from a magma chamber below the surface. All the processes involved in this activity go by the name volcanism, and the study of them is called volcanology.

paragraphs.heading: Sorting by plate setting
paragraphs.text: Earth's rigid outer shell, the lithosphere, is broken into sixteen larger plates and several smaller ones. They move all the time at a slow pace, and most volcanic activity on Earth happens along their boundaries. Volcanoes are most often found where plates are pulling apart or coming together. Those that result from plates pulling apart are usually nonexplosive, while those that result from plates coming together cause violent eruptions. Where two plates slide past one another, volcanoes are usually not created.

paragraphs.heading: Where plates pull apart
paragraphs.text: At mid-ocean ridges two plates move away from each other, and hot mantle rock creeps up beneath the thinned ocean crust. As the pressure on the rising rock drops, part of it melts. That causes volcanism and makes new ocean crust. Most boundaries of this kind lie at the bottom of the oceans, so most volcanic activity on Earth is under the sea. Iceland is a volcanic island formed where the ridge stands above sea level.

paragraphs.heading: Where plates collide
paragraphs.text: A subduction zone is a place where two plates collide, usually an oceanic plate and a continental one. The oceanic plate dives beneath the continental plate. Water released from the diving plate lowers the melting temperature of the mantle above it, and magma forms. This magma is high in silica and extremely viscous, so it often cools and hardens at depth without reaching the surface. When it does reach the surface, a volcano forms. Chains of these volcanoes, called volcanic arcs, border subduction zones.

paragraphs.heading: Away from plate boundaries
paragraphs.text: Volcanic areas called hotspots are thought to be formed by mantle plumes. A plume is hypothesized to be a column of hot material that rises from the boundary between Earth's core and mantle. Plates move across a plume, so each volcano becomes inactive as it drifts off, and new volcanoes appear where the plate advances over the plume. The Hawaiian Islands are thought to have formed this way. The plume hypothesis has been questioned, however.

paragraphs.heading: Sorting by activity
paragraphs.text: Volcanoes are also labelled by how often they erupt. An active volcano has a history of volcanism and is likely to erupt again. A dormant one has not erupted in a long time, generally taken to mean since about 12,000 years ago, but may erupt again. An extinct one has no magma source and cannot erupt at all. These categories may overlap for certain volcanoes. Another split is between volcanoes with more than one period of activity and those that become extinct after erupting exactly once.

paragraphs.heading: Effects and other worlds
paragraphs.text: Large eruptions can affect the temperature of the atmosphere. Ash and sulfuric acid droplets block out the Sun and cool Earth's troposphere. In the past, large eruptions have been followed by volcanic winters that caused catastrophic famines. Earth is not the only planet with volcanoes: they are very numerous on Venus, and Mars has significant ones.
